They call tools over MCP, delegate to other agents over A2A, and act inside business systems. The best agent gateways sit on that path and decide who can do what. This list compares 13 of them on traffic coverage, identity, deployment and price. What is an agent gateway? An agent gateway is a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see, and logs every call. A plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. An agent gateway adds MCP tool governance, agent identity and, increasingly, A2A traffic control. Our ranking below is editorial and weighs 5 criteria: traffic coverage, identity and authorization, deployment options, maturity, and price transparency. How the 13 best agent gateways rank 1. Kong AI Gateway Kong governs LLM, MCP and A2A traffic from 1 control plane. Version 2.0 moved AI features into first-class Providers, Models, MCP Servers and Agents entities . Best for: teams already running Kong for API management. Watch out: the 2.x architecture needs a Konnect control plane. Arcade notes the MCP OAuth2 plugin is still Tech Preview. 2. Bifrost (Maxim AI) Bifrost is an Apache 2.0 Go gateway covering models, MCP tools and A2A agents in 1 deployment. Maxim reports 10,000+ models across 25+ providers. Its benchmark claims 11 µs mean overhead at 5,000 RPS . Best for: self-hosted, in-VPC or air-gapped teams that want all 3 traffic types. Watch out: SSO, SCIM and token exchange are Enterprise-only. An independent review notes the 11 µs figure excludes HTTP handling and JSON marshalling. 3. Gravitee AI Gateway Gravitee runs an LLM Proxy, MCP Proxy and A2A Proxy on 1 runtime. All 3 share 1 authentication, policy and OpenTelemetry chain. The A2A Proxy supports RFC 8693 token exchange and skill-level authorization. Best for: enterprises that want agent identity modeled alongside existing APIs. Watch out: Maxim lists Agent Management from $2,500 per month. The A2A Proxy needs Enterprise Edition. 4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway AgentCore Gateway gives agents 1 managed endpoint for tools, models and other agents . It adds semantic tool search, Cedar policies and on-behalf-of token exchange. Pricing starts at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations . Best for: AWS-native teams using IAM, CloudWatch and Bedrock Guardrails. Watch out: AWS-only. A2A is HTTP passthrough, per Maxim . Search calls cost $0.025 per 1,000 , 5x the invoke rate. 5. Arcade.dev Arcade is an actions runtime, not a model router. Per Arcade , it checks the overlap of user and agent permissions on every action. Credentials never reach the LLM. It lists 8,000+ agent-optimized tools. Best for: agents that write to Salesforce, Gmail or Slack on a user’s behalf. Watch out: no model routing, so pair it with an LLM gateway. Pricing is $25 per month plus $0.10 per auth event and $0.01 per tool call. 6. Prisma AIRS AI Gateway (formerly Portkey) Palo Alto Networks completed its Portkey acquisition in May 2026. The gateway reached GA inside Prisma AIRS in July 2026. Palo Alto describes it as a unified LLM, MCP and A2A gateway with 1 enforcement point. It runs in SaaS and hybrid models . Best for: security teams that want runtime inspection on every prompt. Watch out: pricing is not public. Arcade advises verifying delegated auth and audit depth for agent actions. 7. Azure API Management Microsoft’s AI gateway extends API Management to model APIs, MCP servers and A2A agent APIs. It can expose REST APIs as MCP servers and front existing MCP servers. Best for: Microsoft-centric API teams. Watch out: A2A support is preview, JSON-RPC only, and limited to v2 tiers. 8. Google Cloud Agent Gateway Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It assigns each agent a SPIFFE ID and can apply Model Armor to prompts and responses. Maxim lists up to 5,000 governed resources per gateway. Best for: teams building on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Watch out: Maxim reports cross-cloud support as “coming soon.” Model routing and fallback are not documented. 9. IBM ContextForge ContextForge is an Apache 2.0 registry and proxy that federates MCP, REST, gRPC and A2A. It exposes agents as MCP tools and, per Maxim , deploys via Helm. Best for: free, MCP-first, self-hosted Kubernetes setups. Watch out: no published commercial support. IBM recommends upgrading to v1.1.1 after security bulletins covering v1.0.0 to v1.1.0. 10. Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) Envoy AI Gateway became Agent Router and joined the Agentic AI Foundation in September 2026. It offers an OpenAI-compatible API plus an MCP gateway on Envoy. Best for: Kubernetes teams already on Envoy Gateway. Watch out: A2A is preview and JSON-RPC only. Maxim notes no built-in guardrails. 11. Composio Composio is an MCP gateway and SaaS integration layer with managed OAuth and per-user connected accounts. Arcade lists a free tier of 100,000 tool calls per month and Pro from $29. Best for: fast access to a large prebuilt SaaS catalog. Watch out: Arcade notes sessions are discoverable by default unless allowlisted. 12. TrueFoundry TrueFoundry combines an LLM Gateway and centralized MCP access with training and deployment tooling. Pro costs $25 per user per month , with 20,000 requests and tool calls per user. Best for: ML teams that want gateway and MLOps in 1 platform. Watch out: the client-credentials MCP flow uses a shared identity, not the user’s, Arcade notes . 13. Obot Obot is an open-source platform bundling an MCP Gateway, LLM Gateway and device monitoring. It supports per-user auth, OAuth token exchange and audit logs. Best for: IT teams rolling out MCP servers to employees. Watch out: self-hosting alone does not settle downstream authorization, Arcade notes . Optimized prompts score 56.0 versus 44.6 for the best hand-written harness on Continual Learning Bench. The post Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Test score Database Codebase Spectrum Average No memory 7.5 31.8 21.9 20.4 Compaction 39.8 36.9 34.6 37.1 Generic harness 32.3 33.5 42.5 36.1 Best human-written 47.9 43.7 42.1 44.6 Optimized harness 53.8 64.3 49.9 56.0 SFT on generic trajectories 31.6 37.5 43.6 37.6 SFT on optimized trajectories (generic prompts) 37.7 45.1 46.5 43.1 Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. How does it compare with ALMA, MemEvolve and Harness-Zero? Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. Feature Self-Improving Memory ALMA MemEvolve Harness-Zero Org FAIR at Meta, UW, JHU Xiong, Hu, Clune OPPO AI Agent Team, LV-NUS Peking University, Google, HKUST What is searched LOAD/OFFLOAD memory prompts Memory designs as Python code Memory architecture and contents Full agent harness Trains weights Yes, LoRA rank 64 No No Yes, LoRA SFT Models Kimi-K2.6 (agent and meta agent) GPT-5 meta agent, GPT-5-nano/mini task agent GPT-5-mini (plus DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2) Qwen3.5-9B student Benchmarks Continual Learning Bench (3 tasks) ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack GAIA, WebWalkerQA, xBench-DeepSearch, TaskCraft SpreadsheetBench Verified, AppWorld, USPTO Retrosynthesis Headline result 56.0 vs 44.6 best human harness; 43.1 distilled 53.9% vs 41.1% no memory (GPT-5-mini) Up to 17.06% gains 23.3% to 44.3% with harness removed Code Not released GitHub GitHub GitHub Harness-Zero is the closest match, but it uses a separate agent to correct the student. Distillation keeps part of the gain: 43.1 vs 37.6 with generic prompts. 37 of 44 meta-agent revisions failed, so evaluation and selection matter.
